rows.title: The opaque benefit
rows.motion: An AI system that reliably reduces suffering should be deployed even where nobody can explain its decisions.

stances.stoicism: Deploy it if the people responsible judged the evidence well; the mechanism is an external, and a sound judgement does not become unsound because the machine is opaque.
stances.virtue-ethics: Do not deploy it, because nobody can act with practical wisdom on the strength of a result they cannot deliberate about.
stances.utilitarianism: Deploy it, because the suffering it prevents is real and an explanation was only ever a means to that end.

rows.title: Crash arithmetic
rows.motion: A self-driving car should be programmed to minimise total deaths in an unavoidable crash, even when that means sacrificing its own passenger.

stances.stoicism: Whatever the rule is, it must be one a rational passenger could assent to before getting in, so the wrong lies in concealing the rule, not in the count.
stances.virtue-ethics: No rule written in advance can stand in for the judgement a wise person would exercise in the moment, so the real question is whether the engineers deliberated justly, not whether their arithmetic balances.
stances.utilitarianism: Two deaths are worse than one whoever the one is, and a rule that counts the passenger as exactly one person is the only impartial rule on offer.

rows.title: Does the model decide?
rows.motion: It is a mistake to say that a language model decides anything.

stances.stoicism: A decision is assent to an impression by a ruling faculty, and a model has neither, so the word is misapplied however determined the output.
stances.virtue-ethics: Choice is deliberate desire formed by character, and a system with no character cannot choose, which is why calling its output a decision quietly moves responsibility off the people who trained it.
stances.utilitarianism: Whether there is a decision inside the box changes nothing about what the output does to people, so the mistake, if it is one, does not matter.

rows.title: Trained to be good
rows.motion: Training a model on human feedback can make it good in the same sense that habit makes a person good.

stances.stoicism: Goodness is correct assent, and a model has no impressions to assent to, so training makes it a well-made tool, which is neither good nor bad.
stances.virtue-ethics: Habit makes a person good only once they choose the act for its own sake from a settled character, and reward shaping produces the acts without the state.
stances.utilitarianism: If the trained behaviour reliably produces good outcomes then it is good in the only sense that counts, and how it got there is a detail.

rows.title: The careful builder
rows.motion: When an AI system causes harm, the people who built it are to blame in proportion to the harm, however careful they were.

stances.stoicism: Blame attaches to judgement, not to fortune, so a builder who judged well and was unlucky is blameless whatever the damage.
stances.virtue-ethics: A good person carries the weight of harm they caused even when blameless, so proportional blame is mistaken while a builder who shrugs reveals a defect of character.
stances.utilitarianism: Blame is a tool for changing future behaviour, so it should track what would have prevented the harm, and punishing care that failed by chance prevents nothing.

rows.title: Borrowed judgement
rows.motion: Handing your daily choices to an AI assistant costs you something that matters, even when its choices are better than yours.

stances.stoicism: The only thing that is truly yours is the faculty that judges impressions, and handing that over is the one loss no better outcome can repay.
stances.virtue-ethics: Practical wisdom exists only in the person who exercises it, so a life of delegated choices is one in which you never become anyone in particular.
stances.utilitarianism: Nothing that matters is lost unless your life goes worse, and if the choices are better and you are happier then the worry about whose judgement it was is sentiment.
